course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

quiz.title: Unit 2 SAQ 01
quiz.headline: Why racial slavery took hold
quiz.prompt: Using the sources above, answer (a), (b), and (c).
quiz.instructions: Answer (a), (b), and (c). Each part is worth one point. Answer the question directly, support it with specific historical evidence, and explain how the evidence supports your answer. Describe means more than mentioning a term; explain means showing how or why.
quiz.note: Original Page One practice in AP format. Rubric criteria follow the College Board's AP history rubrics; scoring here is your own self-assessment, not an official score.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 2.6, KC-2.2.II.B: as chattel slavery became the dominant labor system, new laws created a strict racial system
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing historians who emphasize planters' demand for labor in the origins of racial slavery
stimulusBlocks.text: Interpretation A. Racial slavery took hold in the English colonies mainly because of labor needs. In the early 1600s, Chesapeake planters depended on English indentured servants. As fewer servants arrived from England, and as more of those who did arrive survived to demand land of their own, planters turned to enslaved Africans, who could be held for life and whose children could be held as well. Colonial legislatures then wrote slave codes that protected this investment by making slavery lifelong, hereditary, and tied to race. On this view, planters' demand for a permanent workforce produced racial slavery, and racial ideas were used to justify it afterward.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 2.6, KC-2.2.II.B: as chattel slavery became the dominant labor system, new laws created a strict racial system
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing historians who emphasize English attitudes toward Africans in the origins of racial slavery
stimulusBlocks.text: Interpretation B. Racial slavery took hold in the English colonies mainly because of English attitudes toward Africans. Before slavery was widespread, English colonists already described Africans as different and inferior because of their color, their religion, and their origins. Courts in the 1640s sometimes punished Africans more harshly than white servants, and later laws banned marriage between the groups and made slavery pass from mother to child. On this view, prejudice made it easy for planters to hold Africans in permanent bondage, and the laws that made slavery racial grew out of those beliefs, not only out of economic demand.

scaffold.label: Answer
scaffold.text: Respond directly to the task verb: identify, describe, explain, or compare.

scaffold.label: Prove
scaffold.text: Name a specific event, development, or circumstance from the period in the prompt.

scaffold.label: Explain
scaffold.text: Show how or why the evidence answers the question.

parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE important difference between Interpretation A and Interpretation B of the origins of racial slavery in the English colonies.
criteria: Names what each interpretation emphasizes: planters' demand for labor for A and English prejudice for B.
Describes the difference rather than only naming two topics.

model.answer: Interpretation A argues that planters' need for labor produced racial slavery, while Interpretation B argues that English prejudice toward Africans produced it.
model.prove: A says that as fewer English servants arrived, planters turned to enslaved Africans who could be held for life, and that racial ideas justified the choice afterward. B says colonists already regarded Africans as inferior, so laws made slavery racial because of those beliefs.
model.explain: The difference is whether economic demand or existing prejudice was the main cause of racial slavery.

parts.alternatives: A response can also note that A treats racial ideas as a justification that followed slavery, while B treats them as a cause that came before it.

parts.prompt: Briefly explain how ONE specific historical event, development, or circumstance from the period 1607–1754 that is not specifically mentioned in the passages could be used to support Interpretation A.
criteria: Names a specific event or circumstance from 1607–1754 that is not in the passages.
Explains how it shows labor demand leading to the use of enslaved Africans.

model.answer: The growth of tobacco and rice production increased planters' demand for a permanent workforce.
model.prove: As tobacco expanded in the Chesapeake and rice and indigo grew in South Carolina, planters bought rising numbers of enslaved Africans, and the plantation systems of the southern Atlantic coast came to depend on them.
model.explain: This supports Interpretation A because it shows planters turning to enslaved labor when their crops required more workers than indentured servants could supply.

parts.alternatives: A response can also use the demand for labor on the sugar plantations of the West Indies, where most enslaved Africans were sent, if it connects that demand to the choice of enslaved workers.

parts.prompt: Briefly explain how ONE specific historical event, development, or circumstance from the period 1607–1754 that is not specifically mentioned in the passages could be used to support Interpretation B.
criteria: Names a specific event or circumstance from 1607–1754 that is not in the passages.
Explains how it shows prejudice shaping the treatment of Africans.

model.answer: A 1640 Virginia court case punished an African runaway more harshly than white runaways.
model.prove: After three servants escaped, the court added years to the sentences of the two white servants but sentenced John Punch, an African, to serve for life.
model.explain: The different punishments show that officials treated Africans differently before slavery was widespread, which supports Interpretation B's claim that prejudice shaped slavery.

parts.alternatives: A response can also use Virginia's laws banning marriage between English people and Africans, if it explains how they reflect English attitudes about race.
